newsitem.title: USA: Pacific Bell to market ISDN aggressively.
newsitem.headline: Pacific Bell to market ISDN aggressively.

text.p: Pacific Telesis Group's Pacific Bell unit said Friday it would launch a major advertising campaign to promote its ISDN services after California regulators approved a rate increase for the service.

Tom Bayless, director of switched digital services for Pacific Bell, said Friday's decision by the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) removed uncertainty for both the company and its customers.

"We are about to launch a major advertising media campaign throughout California...starting next week," Bayless said, saying the campaign would include television and newspaper advertisements. "Now this is behind us we are going to be aggressively marketing the product," he added.

Bayless said Pacific Bell now has 115,000 ISDN customers and aimed to have 200,000 customers installed by the end of this year. He said ISDN is available to 97 percent of the 10 million homes the company serves in central and northern California.

The commission approved increases in Pacific Bell's residential ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) monthly rate to $29.50 from $24.50. The business rate will rise to $33.25 from $25.75. Pacific Bell had asked for an $8 increase for both business and residential customers.
Bayless said Pacific Bell accepted the commission's decision on rates and thought it was fair. He expected the new rates to take effect within a month to two months.

The commission also ordered Pacific Bell to offer residential customers 200 free hours of off-peak ISDN service per month. After 200 hours, customers will be charged the normal hourly usage fee. Pacific Bell had asked the commission to limit the number of free residential hours to 20 per month.
Bayless said he thought the free off-peak hours would be very attractive to customers. "I think that will make this product sell like hot cakes," he said.
ISDN technology is used to increase existing telephone line transmission capabilities. It makes possible simultaneous voice and data transfers over a single phone line.

The commission also criticized Pacific Bell, saying it found the company's residential ISDN customer service to be inadequate. Representatives were hard to reach and poorly trained and customers requesting ISDN service were subjected to unreasonable delays, the commission said.
The commission said Pacific Bell must pay certain discounts or credits to customers if it missed service targets.
Bayless said Pacific Bell aimed to make the service better than the commission had asked for and to make the incentives a moot issue.
